title: Subqueries
summary_md: Scalar, IN, EXISTS, correlated and derived-table subqueries: when each applies, the NULL traps, and the MySQL restrictions interviewers probe.

sections.heading: Scalar subquery
sections.body_md:
- A scalar subquery returns **one column, at most one row**, and can be used anywhere a single value fits: `WHERE`, `SELECT` list, `HAVING`, `CASE`.
- **Zero rows -> NULL** (not an error). **More than one row -> error** (MySQL 1242, SQL Server 512).
- With `=` it returns every tied row, not just one (see the Engineering example).

syntax.mysql: (SELECT expr FROM t WHERE ... )   -- exactly one column, <= 1 row
syntax.tsql: (SELECT expr FROM t WHERE ... )   -- same; use TOP 1 / MAX() to force a single row

args.name: expr
args.meaning: The single column returned. Two columns is a syntax error.

args.name: WHERE ...
args.meaning: Must narrow to one row, or use an aggregate (MAX, AVG, COUNT) to collapse to one.

examples.title: Above the company average
examples.explain_md: `AVG` ignores Jon's NULL salary, so the average is over 9 people (125000). Ana, Ben and Cara beat it.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: Scalar subquery in the SELECT list
examples.explain_md: The inner query runs once (it is not correlated) and its single value is reused on every row.
examples.mysql:
SELECT order_id, amount,
       ROUND(100.0 * amount / (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'), 1) AS pct_of_completed
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT order_id, amount,
       ROUND(100.0 * amount / (SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed'), 1) AS pct_of_completed
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'
ORDER BY order_id;

examples.title: No matching row gives NULL
examples.explain_md: Nobody works in Legal, so the subquery yields NULL; wrap in `COALESCE` for a default.
examples.mysql:
SELECT (SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Legal') AS raw_value,
       COALESCE((SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Legal'), 'none') AS safe_value;
examples.tsql:
SELECT (SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Legal') AS raw_value,
       COALESCE((SELECT name FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Legal'), 'none') AS safe_value;

examples.title: = returns all tied rows
examples.explain_md: Ben and Cara tie on the Engineering maximum, so `=` against a scalar MAX returns both.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'Engineering'
  AND salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Engineering')
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE dept = 'Engineering'
  AND salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Engineering')
ORDER BY emp_id;

pitfalls_md: `= (SELECT ...)` that matches several rows errors out at runtime, often only after data grows. Use `IN`, an aggregate, or `LIMIT 1` / `TOP 1` with an `ORDER BY`.
A NULL salary never passes `salary > (SELECT AVG(...))`: the comparison is UNKNOWN, so the row is dropped.

sections.heading: IN and NOT IN subqueries
sections.body_md:
- `x IN (SELECT y ...)` is true if `x` equals any value the subquery returns.
- **`NOT IN` + a NULL in the list = no rows at all**: `x <> NULL` is UNKNOWN for every `x`. The classic interview trap.
- Fix with `WHERE y IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery, or use `NOT EXISTS`.

args.name: expr
args.meaning: Outer value (MySQL also allows a tuple: `(a, b) IN (SELECT x, y ...)`).

args.name: SELECT col
args.meaning: Exactly one column (as many columns as the tuple).

examples.title: Customers with a completed order
examples.explain_md: Customer 6 never ordered, so is missing. Duplicates in the subquery do not duplicate outer rows.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed')
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed')
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: Customers with no orders
examples.explain_md: `orders.customer_id` has no NULLs, so `NOT IN` is safe here and returns customer 6.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
ORDER BY customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)
ORDER BY customer_id;

examples.title: NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing
examples.explain_md: Ana's `manager_id` is NULL, so the list contains a NULL and the result is **empty**, even though several people manage nobody.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)
ORDER BY emp_id;

examples.title: The fix: filter the NULL out
examples.explain_md: Same question with `IS NOT NULL` in the subquery: the five people who manage nobody.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL)
ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL)
ORDER BY emp_id;

pitfalls_md: SQL Server has no row-value `(a, b) IN (SELECT ...)`; use `EXISTS` for multi-column matches.
Default to `NOT EXISTS` over `NOT IN`: it is NULL-safe and optimises at least as well.

sections.heading: EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
sections.body_md:
- `EXISTS (subquery)` is true if the subquery returns **at least one row**; the select list is irrelevant (`SELECT 1` by convention).
- It short-circuits on the first match and is **NULL-safe**, which makes `NOT EXISTS` the right anti-join.
- Almost always **correlated**: the subquery references the outer row.

syntax.mysql: [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.key = outer.key AND ...)
syntax.tsql: [NOT] EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE t.key = outer.key AND ...)

args.name: SELECT 1
args.meaning: Select list is ignored; `1`, `*` and a column behave the same.

args.name: t.key = outer.key
args.meaning: The correlation: ties the subquery to the current outer row. Forget it and EXISTS is true for every row (or none).

examples.title: Customers with a completed order of 100 or more
examples.explain_md: The subquery is correlated on `customer_id`. Customers 1, 3, 4 and 5 qualify.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.status = 'completed'
                AND o.amount >= 100)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1
              FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id
                AND o.status = 'completed'
                AND o.amount >= 100)
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: NOT EXISTS survives the NULL manager
examples.explain_md: Same question as the broken `NOT IN` example, now correct: employees nobody reports to.
examples.mysql:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.emp_id)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees r WHERE r.manager_id = e.emp_id)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

examples.title: EXISTS as a yes/no flag
examples.explain_md: `EXISTS` is a predicate, so wrap it in `CASE` to expose it as a column.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.name,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                         WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'cancelled')
            THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS had_cancellation
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.name,
       CASE WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                         WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.status = 'cancelled')
            THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS had_cancellation
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

pitfalls_md: Missing correlation predicate: `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders)` is true for all customers as soon as orders has one row.

sections.heading: Correlated subqueries
sections.body_md:
- A correlated subquery references a column of the outer query, so conceptually it **re-runs for every outer row**.
- Optimisers often rewrite it into a join, but assume per-row cost on big tables.
- Alias both sides (`o` and `i`) so the correlation is unambiguous.

syntax.mysql: SELECT ... FROM t o WHERE o.col > (SELECT AGG(i.col) FROM t i WHERE i.grp = o.grp)
syntax.tsql: SELECT ... FROM t o WHERE o.col > (SELECT AGG(i.col) FROM t i WHERE i.grp = o.grp)

args.name: o
args.meaning: Outer alias; the subquery may read its columns.

args.name: i
args.meaning: Inner alias for the same table; never reuse the outer alias.

examples.title: Orders above that customer's own average
examples.explain_md: The inner `AVG` is recomputed per customer. Customer 2's 45.50 and 60.00 beat their 37.625 average.
examples.mysql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.amount
FROM orders o
WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount)
                  FROM orders i
                  WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER BY o.order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.amount
FROM orders o
WHERE o.amount > (SELECT AVG(i.amount)
                  FROM orders i
                  WHERE i.customer_id = o.customer_id)
ORDER BY o.order_id;

examples.title: Paid above the department average
examples.explain_md: Marketing's average is Ivy alone (NULL Jon skipped), so nobody beats it; Ana is her own department.
examples.mysql:
SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employees x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

examples.title: Correlated subquery in the SELECT list
examples.explain_md: `COUNT` gives 0 for customer 6 but `MAX` gives NULL: only `COUNT` turns 'no rows' into 0.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)        FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS n_orders,
       (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*)        FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS n_orders,
       (SELECT MAX(order_date) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id) AS last_order
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

pitfalls_md: Self-correlation without aliases (`WHERE customer_id = customer_id`) compares the inner column to itself: always true.

sections.heading: Derived tables in FROM
sections.body_md:
- A subquery in `FROM` acts as a temporary table for one statement: aggregate first, then join or filter the result.
- **An alias is mandatory** in both MySQL and SQL Server.
- Use it to filter on a window function result or on an aggregate-of-aggregate.

args.name: (SELECT ...)
args.meaning: Any query; every output column needs a unique name (alias expressions).

examples.title: Aggregate, then join
examples.explain_md: Roll orders up to one row per customer in a derived table, then join to names.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.name, t.n_orders, t.total
FROM customers c
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, SUM(amount) AS total
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS t
  ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.name, t.n_orders, t.total
FROM customers c
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders, SUM(amount) AS total
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS t
  ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Average of per-customer totals
examples.explain_md: You cannot write `AVG(SUM(x))`; the inner `SUM` has to live in a derived table.
examples.mysql:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(t.total), 2) AS avg_customer_total
FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS t;
examples.tsql:
SELECT ROUND(AVG(t.total), 2) AS avg_customer_total
FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total
      FROM orders
      WHERE status = 'completed'
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS t;

examples.title: Filter on a window function
examples.explain_md: `WHERE rnk = 1` is illegal at the same query level as the window; push the window into a derived table. Ben and Cara tie.
examples.mysql:
SELECT r.dept, r.name, r.salary
FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary,
             RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
      FROM employees) AS r
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY r.dept, r.name;
examples.tsql:
SELECT r.dept, r.name, r.salary
FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary,
             RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
      FROM employees) AS r
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY r.dept, r.name;

pitfalls_md: Unnamed expressions inside a derived table (`SELECT COUNT(*)` with no alias) cannot be referenced outside it, and SQL Server rejects them outright.
SQL Server forbids `ORDER BY` inside a derived table unless you also use `TOP` / `OFFSET`.

sections.heading: Subquery vs JOIN vs window
sections.body_md:
- **Existence / absence** ("has any", "has none"): `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` (or `LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL`). Never needs a DISTINCT.
- **Need columns from the other table**: `JOIN`. Beware row multiplication when the other side has many matches.
- **Compare a row to an aggregate of its group**: a window (`AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)`) reads the table once; a correlated subquery or a join to a grouped derived table reads it twice.
- **Top-N per group / latest per key**: window `ROW_NUMBER` / `RANK`.
- Interviewers like hearing two approaches and the trade-off; the last two examples return identical rows.

examples.title: Anti-join with LEFT JOIN
examples.explain_md: Same answer as `NOT EXISTS` / `NOT IN`: customers with no orders. Test the **right** table's key for NULL.
examples.mysql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;

examples.title: Above own average, window version
examples.explain_md: Same rows as the correlated example, one scan. The window must sit in a subquery/CTE before it can be filtered.
examples.mysql:
SELECT x.order_id, x.customer_id, x.amount
FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
             AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS cust_avg
      FROM orders) AS x
WHERE x.amount > x.cust_avg
ORDER BY x.order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT x.order_id, x.customer_id, x.amount
FROM (SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount,
             AVG(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS cust_avg
      FROM orders) AS x
WHERE x.amount > x.cust_avg
ORDER BY x.order_id;

examples.title: Above own average, join version
examples.explain_md: Join to a grouped derived table; each customer's average is computed once.
examples.mysql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS cust_avg
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS a
  ON a.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > a.cust_avg
ORDER BY o.order_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.amount
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, AVG(amount) AS cust_avg
      FROM orders
      GROUP BY customer_id) AS a
  ON a.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.amount > a.cust_avg
ORDER BY o.order_id;

sections.heading: MySQL limits and the derived-table workaround
sections.body_md:
- **No `LIMIT` inside `IN` / `ANY` / `ALL` / `SOME` subqueries** in MySQL (error 1235). `LIMIT` is fine in derived tables and scalar subqueries. SQL Server allows `TOP` there.
- **You cannot select from the table you are updating or deleting** in the same statement (MySQL error 1093). Wrap the inner query in a derived table so it is materialised first. SQL Server has no such restriction.
- Pattern for both: `WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM t ... LIMIT n) AS s)`.

syntax.tsql:
UPDATE employees SET salary = salary * 1.05
WHERE emp_id IN (SELECT emp_id FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Sales');   -- allowed

args.name: AS s
args.meaning: The derived table forces MySQL to materialise the inner rows before the UPDATE starts.

examples.title: Top 3 earners via IN
examples.explain_md: MySQL needs the extra derived table `top3`; SQL Server puts `TOP (3)` straight in the subquery. Ties are broken on `emp_id` so the three rows are stable.
examples.mysql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (SELECT emp_id
                 FROM (SELECT emp_id
                       FROM employees
                       ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id
                       LIMIT 3) AS top3)
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE emp_id IN (SELECT TOP (3) emp_id
                 FROM employees
                 ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id)
ORDER BY salary DESC, emp_id;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL: `IN (SELECT ... LIMIT 3)` raises error 1235; the inner derived table is the workaround. SQL Server accepts `TOP` inside the subquery.

examples.title: Preview the rows an UPDATE would touch
examples.explain_md: A self-referencing UPDATE/DELETE needs the same derived-table wrapper in MySQL. Shown as a SELECT so it stays checkable; the UPDATE form is in the syntax box.
examples.mysql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE e.emp_id IN (SELECT s.emp_id
                   FROM (SELECT emp_id FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Sales') AS s)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;
examples.tsql:
SELECT e.emp_id, e.name
FROM employees e
WHERE e.emp_id IN (SELECT s.emp_id
                   FROM (SELECT emp_id FROM employees WHERE dept = 'Sales') AS s)
ORDER BY e.emp_id;

pitfalls_md: A CTE or `UPDATE ... JOIN` also avoids error 1093 in MySQL 8.
